answers.question: For the Prototype pattern, what is the shallow-clone trap, and why is a copy constructor often preferred over `Cloneable` (Bloch's criticism)?
answers.shortTitle: Prototype pattern — the shallow-clone trap, and why a copy constructor beats Cloneable (Bloch's criticism)

s1_definition.profdef: The Prototype pattern creates new objects by copying an existing instance, called the prototype, rather than constructing them from scratch. It is useful when object creation is expensive or complex and you already have a fully configured instance to copy. In Java the historical mechanism was the `Cloneable` interface with `Object.clone`, but that approach produces a shallow copy by default and has well-known design flaws, so the preferred modern technique is a copy constructor or a static copy factory that performs an explicit, deep, and type-safe copy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a standard loan-application template that is already filled with the bank's default terms, interest clauses, and formatting. When Rajesh applies, instead of typing a whole new form from blank paper, the clerk photocopies the template and just changes the applicant details. That photocopy-the-template approach is the Prototype pattern. But there is a catch: if the template has a stapled booklet of sub-documents and the "photocopy" only copies the cover page while still pointing to the same shared booklet, then editing Rajesh's booklet accidentally changes Priya's too. That shared-booklet problem is the shallow-clone trap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Prototype copies an existing object to make a new one; the shallow-clone trap is when the copy still shares the original's inner mutable objects, and a copy constructor avoids the mess of Cloneable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Prototype pattern creates new objects by copying an existing instance, called the prototype, rather than constructing them from scratch. It is useful when object creation is expensive or complex and you already have a fully configured instance to copy. In Java the historical mechanism was the `Cloneable` interface with `Object.clone`, but that approach produces a shallow copy by default and has well-known design flaws, so the preferred modern technique is a copy constructor or a static copy factory that performs an explicit, deep, and type-safe copy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a standard loan-application template that is already filled with the bank's default terms, interest clauses, and formatting. When Rajesh applies, instead of typing a whole new form from blank paper, the clerk photocopies the template and just changes the applicant details. That photocopy-the-template approach is the Prototype pattern. But there is a catch: if the template has a stapled booklet of sub-documents and the "photocopy" only copies the cover page while still pointing to the same shared booklet, then editing Rajesh's booklet accidentally changes Priya's too. That shared-booklet problem is the shallow-clone trap.

**One line to remember:** Prototype copies an existing object to make a new one; the shallow-clone trap is when the copy still shares the original's inner mutable objects, and a copy constructor avoids the mess of Cloneable.

sections.s2_technical:
The Prototype pattern answers "I need another object just like this one." Rather than calling a complicated constructor and reconfiguring everything, you copy a prototype that is already set up. This is handy for expensive-to-build objects or when you want several variations of a configured baseline.

The **shallow-clone trap** is the central danger. A shallow copy duplicates the top-level object but copies only the references of its fields, not the objects those references point to. So if an `Account` holds a `List<Transaction>`, a shallow copy gives you a new `Account` whose list field points to the very same list object as the original. Now adding a transaction to the copy also adds it to the original, because they share one list. In banking this is catastrophic — cloning an account to make a what-if scenario would silently corrupt the real account's transaction history. A **deep copy** fixes this by recursively copying the inner mutable objects too, so the copy has its own independent list. The trap is that `Object.clone`, the default mechanism, produces a shallow copy unless you manually copy each mutable field yourself.

Now the historical mechanism and its problems. Java's `Cloneable` interface is a **marker interface** with no methods. To make a class cloneable you implement `Cloneable` and override the protected `Object.clone` method, usually calling `super.clone()`. Joshua Bloch, in Effective Java, criticises this design harshly, and interviewers love these points. First, `Cloneable` lacks a `clone` method — it is a marker that merely changes the behaviour of the protected `Object.clone`, which is deeply unusual and confusing. Second, `clone` is declared on `Object` as protected and returns `Object`, so callers need casts and the method is awkward to use. Third, `clone` does not run constructors, so it can produce an object in an invalid state and it bypasses `final` fields — you cannot assign a `final` field inside `clone`, which conflicts with immutability. Fourth, it throws the checked `CloneNotSupportedException` even when you know the class is cloneable, forcing clumsy try-catch. Fifth, the contract between `clone`, `super.clone`, and deep copying is fragile and easy to get wrong, especially with inheritance.

The recommended alternative is a **copy constructor** or a **copy factory**. A copy constructor is simply a constructor that takes an instance of the same class and copies its state, performing deep copies of mutable fields explicitly: `public Account(Account other) { this.id = other.id; this.transactions = new ArrayList<>(other.transactions); }`. A copy factory is the static equivalent, such as `public static Account copyOf(Account other) { ... }`. Bloch recommends these because they do not rely on the error-prone extralinguistic `clone` mechanism, they do not throw unnecessary checked exceptions, they do not require casts, they work properly with `final` fields since they run a real constructor, and they let you convert between related types or interface-based copies. Crucially, you write the deep-copy logic explicitly, so there is no hidden shallow-copy surprise — you see exactly which fields are copied and how.

A senior nuance: for arrays, `clone` is actually fine and idiomatic because arrays have a well-defined, efficient clone. And for genuinely immutable classes, copying is unnecessary — you can safely share the same instance since nothing can mutate it, which is another reason immutability pairs so well with the Prototype idea. In modern Java, records and immutable builders further reduce the need for cloning at all.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to run "what-if" scenarios on Rajesh's account: take his current account with its transaction history and simulate applying a few hypothetical transactions without touching the real account. The first attempt used `Cloneable` and the default shallow `clone`, so the cloned scenario account shared the same transaction list as the real one. When the simulation added a hypothetical transaction, it silently appeared in Rajesh's real history too. This is the shallow-clone trap causing real data corruption.

Problem 2 — We want a copy mechanism that is explicit, safe, works with final fields, and does not force us into awkward checked exceptions and casts. That is exactly what a copy constructor gives, with an explicit deep copy of the transaction list.

In the mini-project we will show both the broken shallow clone and the correct copy constructor. We will build an `Account` holding an id, a holder name, a balance, and a mutable list of transactions. We will first demonstrate the shallow-clone trap by sharing the list and watching the original get corrupted. Then we will provide a proper copy constructor that deep-copies the list, make a scenario copy of Rajesh's account, add a hypothetical transaction to the copy, and show the real account is untouched.

The code contains: a `Transaction` model; an `Account` with a copy constructor; a demonstration of the shallow-copy trap; and the correct deep-copy via copy constructor.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account with two real transactions, and a what-if scenario that adds a hypothetical transaction.

Step 1: We create Rajesh's account and add two real transactions, T1 and T2. The account's transaction list now has two entries.

Step 2: We make a shallow, broken copy whose list field points to the very same list object as the real account. The copy and the original now share one list in memory.

Step 3: We add a hypothetical transaction to the shallow copy. Because both share the same list, the hypothetical transaction also appears in the real account, which now wrongly shows three transactions. This is the shallow-clone trap corrupting live data.

Step 4: We rebuild a clean original, then use the copy constructor. Inside the copy constructor, `new ArrayList<>(other.transactions)` builds a brand-new list containing the same transaction objects but in an independent container. The scenario copy now has its own list.

Step 5: We add the hypothetical transaction to the scenario copy. Only the copy's list grows to three; the real account still shows two. The deep copy via the copy constructor kept the two accounts fully independent, which is the safe and correct behaviour.

```
2026-10-26 10:25:00 [INFO] === SHALLOW copy trap ===
2026-10-26 10:25:00 [SEVERE] After editing shallow copy, REAL account has 3 txns (corrupted!)
2026-10-26 10:25:00 [INFO] === Copy CONSTRUCTOR (deep, safe) ===
2026-10-26 10:25:00 [INFO] Scenario copy has 3 txns, REAL account still has 2 (safe!)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Prototype pattern creates a new object by copying an existing, already-configured instance rather than building it from scratch. It is useful when construction is expensive or complex and you already have a good baseline to copy. The classic banking use is running what-if scenarios: I take a real account and copy it so I can simulate hypothetical transactions without touching the real one.

The central danger is the shallow-clone trap. A shallow copy duplicates the top-level object but only copies the references of its fields, so if an account holds a list of transactions, the shallow copy's list field points to the very same list object as the original. The moment I add a hypothetical transaction to the copy, it also appears in the real account, because they share one list. In my project this actually corrupted live transaction history. A deep copy fixes it by recursively copying the inner mutable objects so the copy has its own independent list.

This is where I bring in Joshua Bloch's criticism of Cloneable, which interviewers expect. Cloneable is a marker interface with no clone method, which is confusing because it merely changes the behaviour of the protected Object.clone. The clone method returns Object so you need casts, it does not run a constructor so it can produce an invalid object and cannot assign final fields, it throws a checked CloneNotSupportedException that forces clumsy try-catch, and worst of all it is shallow by default, which is exactly the trap. For all these reasons Bloch recommends a copy constructor or a static copy factory instead.

So in practice I prefer a copy constructor: a constructor that takes another instance and copies its state, explicitly deep-copying mutable fields like the transaction list with a new ArrayList. It is explicit so there is no hidden shallow surprise, it works correctly with final fields because it runs a real constructor, it needs no casts, and it does not throw spurious checked exceptions. I also remember two nuances: for plain arrays, clone is actually fine and idiomatic, and for genuinely immutable classes I do not copy at all, because sharing one instance is perfectly safe when nothing can mutate it.

answers.question: How does Java I/O (`DataInputStream` wrapping `BufferedInputStream` wrapping `GZIPInputStream`...) exemplify the Decorator pattern, and how does it avoid subclass explosion?
answers.shortTitle: How Java I/O streams exemplify the Decorator pattern and avoid subclass explosion

s1_definition.profdef: The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that shares the same interface. Java's I/O stream library is the textbook example: concrete streams like `FileInputStream` provide the raw source, and decorator streams like `BufferedInputStream`, `GZIPInputStream`, and `DataInputStream` each wrap another stream, add one behaviour, and expose the same `InputStream` interface. Because every decorator both is-an `InputStream` and has-an `InputStream`, you can stack them in any order and combination at runtime, which avoids creating a separate subclass for every possible feature combination.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends a daily statement file. The raw file is plain data. Now you want it buffered for speed, compressed to save space, and read as structured numbers. Instead of inventing a special "buffered-compressed-structured" machine, you take the plain file and wrap it: first put it through a buffering layer, then through a decompression layer, then through a structured-reading layer. Each layer is like a clip-on attachment that adds one capability and passes the data along. You can snap the attachments on in any order you need. That snap-on-layers idea is the Decorator pattern, and it is exactly how Java's streams work.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each Java stream decorator wraps another stream of the same type and adds one feature, so you stack capabilities at runtime instead of building a subclass for every combination.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that shares the same interface. Java's I/O stream library is the textbook example: concrete streams like `FileInputStream` provide the raw source, and decorator streams like `BufferedInputStream`, `GZIPInputStream`, and `DataInputStream` each wrap another stream, add one behaviour, and expose the same `InputStream` interface. Because every decorator both is-an `InputStream` and has-an `InputStream`, you can stack them in any order and combination at runtime, which avoids creating a separate subclass for every possible feature combination.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sends a daily statement file. The raw file is plain data. Now you want it buffered for speed, compressed to save space, and read as structured numbers. Instead of inventing a special "buffered-compressed-structured" machine, you take the plain file and wrap it: first put it through a buffering layer, then through a decompression layer, then through a structured-reading layer. Each layer is like a clip-on attachment that adds one capability and passes the data along. You can snap the attachments on in any order you need. That snap-on-layers idea is the Decorator pattern, and it is exactly how Java's streams work.

**One line to remember:** Each Java stream decorator wraps another stream of the same type and adds one feature, so you stack capabilities at runtime instead of building a subclass for every combination.

sections.s2_technical:
The Decorator pattern has four roles. There is a **component** interface or abstract class that defines the common type — in Java I/O this is `InputStream` (and `OutputStream`, `Reader`, `Writer` on the other sides). There is a **concrete component** that is a real source or sink — `FileInputStream`, `ByteArrayInputStream`. There is an abstract **decorator** that both extends the component type and holds a reference to a wrapped component — `FilterInputStream` holds a `protected volatile InputStream in`. And there are **concrete decorators** that add behaviour — `BufferedInputStream`, `DataInputStream`, `GZIPInputStream` (via `InflaterInputStream`).

The key structural trick is that each decorator **is-a `InputStream` and has-a `InputStream`**. Because a decorator extends `InputStream`, it can be used anywhere an `InputStream` is expected, including as the thing another decorator wraps. Because it holds an inner `InputStream`, it can delegate the real work and add its own behaviour around it. That dual relationship is what lets you compose them. For example: `InputStream in = new DataInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream("statement.gz"))));`. Reading from the outermost `DataInputStream` triggers a chain: it asks the buffered stream for bytes, which asks the gzip stream, which asks the file stream, which reads from disk; then decompression happens, then buffering, then interpretation as typed values on the way back out.

Each decorator adds exactly one concern. `FileInputStream` is the source that reads raw bytes from disk. `GZIPInputStream` transparently decompresses. `BufferedInputStream` reads a big chunk into an internal buffer so each small read does not hit the disk, which is a big performance win. `DataInputStream` adds methods to read primitive types, like `readInt`, `readDouble`, and `readUTF`, so you can read structured banking data rather than raw bytes. For example `double balance = dataIn.readDouble();` reads eight bytes and interprets them as a double, while the layers beneath handle buffering and decompression invisibly.

Now the crucial point: **how this avoids subclass explosion.** Imagine you did not have decorators and instead used inheritance to combine features. You would need a `FileInputStream`, then a `BufferedFileInputStream`, a `GzipFileInputStream`, a `DataFileInputStream`, then a `BufferedGzipFileInputStream`, a `BufferedDataFileInputStream`, a `GzipDataFileInputStream`, a `BufferedGzipDataFileInputStream`, and so on for every source and every combination and every ordering. With n independent features the number of combinations grows combinatorially — this is the subclass explosion. The Decorator pattern collapses that: you write one decorator class per feature, and you compose them at runtime in whatever order and combination you need. Three decorator classes give you all the combinations instead of eight-plus subclasses, and adding a fourth feature is one more class, not a doubling of the hierarchy.

Several senior nuances are worth stating. First, order matters: buffering a compressed stream versus compressing a buffered stream behave differently, and the programmer controls that by the wrapping order. Second, closing the outermost stream closes the whole chain, because each decorator's `close` delegates to the inner stream — so you only need one try-with-resources on the outer stream. Third, this flexibility has a cost: the layered design is powerful but the class hierarchy is large and sometimes criticised as hard to learn, and each layer adds a small indirection. Fourth, the same pattern appears on the output side with `DataOutputStream`, `BufferedOutputStream`, `GZIPOutputStream`, and in the character streams with `BufferedReader` wrapping `InputStreamReader`. Recognising this in Java immediately tells an interviewer you understand both the library and the pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores daily account-balance snapshots in a file. The file is large, so the bank compresses it with gzip to save disk. Reading it one byte at a time directly from disk would be painfully slow, and the data is structured — each record is an account id and a balance as typed values, not plain text. So reading this file needs three capabilities at once: decompression, buffering for speed, and structured typed reading. Building a dedicated class for this exact combination would be wasteful and inflexible, especially since tomorrow we might need an uncompressed version or a buffered-but-not-typed version. This is exactly what the Decorator pattern solves — we compose the three capabilities by wrapping streams.

Problem 2 — We want to write the file the same way, stacking a gzip-compressing layer, a buffering layer, and a typed-writing layer, and we want to be able to change the stack easily. We also want closing to be simple, closing the whole chain with one statement.

In the mini-project we will write Rajesh's and Priya's balance snapshots to a gzip-compressed, buffered, structured file by stacking `DataOutputStream` over `BufferedOutputStream` over `GZIPOutputStream` over `FileOutputStream`. Then we will read them back by stacking the mirror-image input decorators. We will log each record read, demonstrating that the typed values come back correctly through all the layers. We will also point out, in comments, the subclass-explosion that inheritance would have caused.

The code contains: a small `balance-snapshot` writer that stacks output decorators, and a reader that stacks input decorators, using try-with-resources so one close tears down the whole chain.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two balance records — SAV2001 with ten lakh and CUR3001 with two and a half lakh — plus an END marker.

Step 1: On writing, we build the output stack. The innermost `FileOutputStream` opens the file for raw bytes. It is wrapped by `GZIPOutputStream`, which will compress whatever flows through it. That is wrapped by `BufferedOutputStream`, which collects writes into a buffer before flushing. The outermost `DataOutputStream` offers typed methods like `writeUTF` and `writeDouble`.

Step 2: We call `out.writeUTF("SAV2001")` and `out.writeDouble(1000000.00)`. The typed bytes flow down: `DataOutputStream` turns them into bytes, `BufferedOutputStream` batches them, `GZIPOutputStream` compresses them, and `FileOutputStream` writes the compressed bytes to disk. The programmer only talks to the outer stream; the layers do their jobs invisibly.

Step 3: Leaving the try-with-resources calls `close` on the outer `DataOutputStream`, which flushes the buffer, finishes the gzip stream, and closes the file — the whole chain shuts down from one statement.

Step 4: On reading, we build the mirror stack. `FileInputStream` reads compressed bytes, `GZIPInputStream` decompresses, `BufferedInputStream` reads ahead in chunks, and `DataInputStream` interprets typed values. We call `in.readUTF()` and `in.readDouble()` and get back the exact account id and balance we wrote.

Step 5: We loop until we read the END marker. Each record comes back correctly through all three decorators, proving the layers compose transparently. Three small decorator classes delivered compression, buffering, and typed I/O in any order we chose, with no combinatorial subclasses.

```
2026-10-26 10:30:00 [INFO] === WRITE: DataOutputStream -> Buffered -> GZIP -> File ===
2026-10-26 10:30:00 [INFO] === READ: DataInputStream -> Buffered -> GZIP -> File ===
2026-10-26 10:30:00 [INFO] Read record -> account=SAV2001 balance=Rs.1000000.0
2026-10-26 10:30:00 [INFO] Read record -> account=CUR3001 balance=Rs.250000.0
2026-10-26 10:30:00 [INFO] Done — 3 decorator classes gave us compression + buffering + typed I/O.
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
The Decorator pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that shares the same interface, and Java's I/O stream library is the textbook example. On the input side the common type is InputStream. FileInputStream is the concrete source that reads raw bytes, and decorators like GZIPInputStream, BufferedInputStream, and DataInputStream each wrap another stream, add exactly one capability, and still expose the InputStream interface.

The structural trick I always highlight is that each decorator is-an InputStream and also has-an InputStream. Because it extends InputStream it can be used anywhere a stream is expected, including as the thing another decorator wraps, and because it holds an inner stream it delegates the real work and adds its own behaviour around it. That dual relationship is what lets me write something like a DataInputStream wrapping a BufferedInputStream wrapping a GZIPInputStream wrapping a FileInputStream, and reading from the outer stream pulls bytes up through the whole chain — the file reads, gzip decompresses, buffering speeds it up, and DataInputStream interprets typed values, all transparently.

The reason this matters is that it avoids subclass explosion. If I tried to combine these features with inheritance, I would need a separate subclass for every combination and ordering — buffered, gzipped, data, buffered-gzipped, buffered-data, gzipped-data, buffered-gzipped-data, and so on — which grows combinatorially with the number of features. The Decorator pattern collapses that: one class per feature, composed at runtime in whatever order I need. Three decorator classes give me every combination, and adding a fourth feature is one more class rather than doubling the hierarchy.

In my banking project I used exactly this to read and write compressed, buffered, structured balance-snapshot files. I stacked DataOutputStream over BufferedOutputStream over GZIPOutputStream over FileOutputStream to write, and the mirror stack to read, using try-with-resources so closing the outer stream tore down the whole chain in one statement. The two nuances I mention are that wrapping order matters, since buffering a compressed stream differs from compressing a buffered one, and that this flexibility costs a somewhat large and sometimes confusing class hierarchy plus a little indirection per layer — a trade-off the Java designers accepted for the composability it provides.

answers.question: Explain the Proxy pattern types (Virtual/lazy, Protection/access-control, Caching, Dynamic/JDK, Remote) and how Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies.
answers.shortTitle: Proxy pattern types (Virtual, Protection, Caching, Dynamic, Remote) and how Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies

s1_definition.profdef: The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real object, so clients cannot tell the difference, but the proxy can add behaviour before or after delegating to the real object — such as lazy creation, access checks, caching, or remote communication. Spring AOP is a large-scale application of this pattern: it wraps your beans in dynamically generated proxies that run cross-cutting concerns like transactions, security, and logging around your actual method calls.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants to speak to the bank's senior loan officer, but he does not talk to the officer directly. Instead he talks to the officer's assistant, who looks and acts like the officer's front desk. The assistant checks Rajesh's appointment (access control), remembers answers to common questions so the officer is not disturbed twice (caching), only calls the officer in when actually needed (lazy), and can even phone a branch in another city on Rajesh's behalf (remote). Rajesh thinks he is dealing with the officer's office directly, but the assistant is a stand-in controlling and enhancing access. That stand-in is a proxy.
s1_definition.oneliner: A proxy is a same-interface stand-in that controls access to the real object and can add lazy creation, security, caching, or remote calls around it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real object, so clients cannot tell the difference, but the proxy can add behaviour before or after delegating to the real object — such as lazy creation, access checks, caching, or remote communication. Spring AOP is a large-scale application of this pattern: it wraps your beans in dynamically generated proxies that run cross-cutting concerns like transactions, security, and logging around your actual method calls.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants to speak to the bank's senior loan officer, but he does not talk to the officer directly. Instead he talks to the officer's assistant, who looks and acts like the officer's front desk. The assistant checks Rajesh's appointment (access control), remembers answers to common questions so the officer is not disturbed twice (caching), only calls the officer in when actually needed (lazy), and can even phone a branch in another city on Rajesh's behalf (remote). Rajesh thinks he is dealing with the officer's office directly, but the assistant is a stand-in controlling and enhancing access. That stand-in is a proxy.

**One line to remember:** A proxy is a same-interface stand-in that controls access to the real object and can add lazy creation, security, caching, or remote calls around it.

sections.s2_technical:
The structure has three roles: a **subject** interface that both the real object and the proxy implement, a **real subject** that does the actual work, and a **proxy** that holds a reference to the real subject and implements the same interface, adding behaviour around the delegation. Because the proxy shares the interface, client code written against the interface works unchanged whether it holds the real object or the proxy.

There are several common **types of proxy**, each adding a different concern. A **virtual proxy** provides lazy initialisation: it defers creating an expensive real object until it is first actually needed. For example, a statement-generation service that is costly to construct is only built the first time someone requests a statement, and the virtual proxy holds a null reference until then. A **protection proxy** enforces access control: it checks the caller's permissions before delegating. In banking, a protection proxy on an account service might verify that only an authorised teller or the account owner can call `withdraw`, rejecting others. A **caching proxy** remembers the results of expensive operations and returns the cached value on repeat calls, so a proxy over a credit-score lookup returns the cached score instead of calling the slow external service again. A **remote proxy** represents an object that lives in another address space or machine, hiding the network communication so the client calls it like a local object — this is how Java RMI stubs and many RPC clients work. A **smart proxy** (smart reference) adds extra actions such as reference counting, logging, or acquiring and releasing locks around access.

Java supports proxies in code through two mechanisms, which is where **dynamic proxies** come in. A static proxy is a class you write by hand that implements the interface and delegates. A **dynamic proxy** is generated at runtime. The **JDK dynamic proxy** uses `java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance`, which creates a proxy object implementing a set of interfaces, routing every method call through an `InvocationHandler.invoke` method where you add your behaviour and then delegate to the target. The important limitation is that JDK dynamic proxies work only when the target implements at least one interface, because the generated proxy implements interfaces, not the concrete class. When there is no interface, Spring and others fall back to **CGLIB**, which generates a runtime subclass of the target class and overrides its methods — this works on concrete classes but cannot proxy final classes or final methods.

Now **how Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies**, which interviewers always probe. When you annotate a method with something like `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, or a custom aspect, Spring does not modify your class. Instead, at startup, Spring wraps your bean in a proxy. If your bean implements an interface, Spring by default creates a JDK dynamic proxy that implements that interface; if it does not implement an interface, Spring uses CGLIB to create a subclass proxy. When another bean calls your method, it is really calling the proxy. The proxy runs the configured advice — for `@Transactional`, it opens a transaction before your method, commits if it returns normally, and rolls back if it throws — and then delegates to your real method. This is exactly the Proxy pattern applied to cross-cutting concerns: transaction management, security checks, caching, and logging are all added around your method without touching your business code.

A critical senior nuance is the **self-invocation problem**. Because the proxy wraps the bean from outside, a call from one method of a bean to another method of the same bean using plain `this.otherMethod()` bypasses the proxy entirely, so annotations like `@Transactional` or `@Cacheable` on that inner method do not take effect. The call did not go through the proxy, so no advice runs. The fixes are to restructure so the annotated method is called from another bean, to inject the bean into itself and call through that reference, or to use `AopContext.currentProxy()`. Another nuance is that JDK proxies are interface-based and CGLIB is subclass-based, so whether your method must be public and non-final depends on the mechanism — CGLIB requires non-final, overridable methods. Understanding this explains many real Spring bugs where an annotation silently does nothing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has an `AccountService` whose `getBalance` calls an expensive, slow backend. Many parts of the system repeatedly ask for the same account's balance within seconds, hammering the backend. We want to cache the result for a short time without changing the business logic of `AccountService`. This is a caching proxy — a stand-in that returns the cached balance on repeat calls and only hits the real service when needed.

Problem 2 — We also want to enforce that only authorised callers can invoke sensitive operations, and we want to add this access check without editing the service. This is a protection proxy. And we want to understand how a dynamic proxy, generated at runtime, can add this behaviour generically rather than hand-writing a proxy class per service, which is how Spring AOP works under the hood.

In the mini-project we will build the `AccountService` interface and its real implementation. We will write a hand-coded caching-and-protection static proxy to show the pattern concretely. Then we will build a JDK dynamic proxy using `Proxy.newProxyInstance` and an `InvocationHandler` that logs and caches around any method, demonstrating the mechanism Spring AOP relies on. We will query Rajesh's balance twice and show the second call is served from cache, and show an unauthorised caller being rejected.

The code contains: an `AccountService` interface and `RealAccountService`; a dynamic-proxy `InvocationHandler` that adds caching and an access check; and a `main` that exercises both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two balance queries for SAV2001 as a teller, and one withdraw attempt as a guest.

Step 1: We create the real `RealAccountService`, then wrap it in a JDK dynamic proxy using `Proxy.newProxyInstance`, passing the interface and an `InvocationHandler`. The returned object implements `AccountService` but is actually the generated proxy. The teller holds this proxy, believing it is the service.

Step 2: The teller calls `getBalance("SAV2001")` the first time. The call goes through the proxy to `invoke`. It is a `getBalance`, the cache is empty, so it is a miss: the handler delegates to the real service, which runs the slow backend, returns ten lakh, and the handler stores it in the cache.

Step 3: The teller calls `getBalance("SAV2001")` again. This time `invoke` finds the value in the cache and returns it immediately without touching the slow backend. The caching proxy saved a backend call.

Step 4: A guest holds a proxy configured with the GUEST role and calls `withdraw`. In `invoke`, the method is `withdraw` and the role is not TELLER, so the handler throws a `SecurityException` before ever delegating to the real service. The protection proxy blocked unauthorised access.

Step 5: Throughout, the real service's business code was never modified. The caching and access control were added purely by the proxy, which is precisely how Spring AOP adds transactions and security around your beans at runtime.

```
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] === Caching proxy: first call hits backend, second is cached ===
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] [REAL] backend fetched balance for SAV2001
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] [PROXY] cache MISS -> stored SAV2001
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] Balance #1: Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] [PROXY] cache HIT for SAV2001
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] Balance #2: Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [INFO] === Protection proxy: unauthorised caller rejected ===
2026-10-26 10:35:00 [WARNING] Access denied for GUEST — role GUEST cannot withdraw
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client holds AccountService (actually a PROXY)
    │ proxy.getBalance("SAV2001")
    ▼
  InvocationHandler.invoke(method=getBalance)
    │
    ├─ cache HIT  → return cached value (NO backend call)
    │
    └─ cache MISS → method.invoke(target) → RealAccountService
                       │ slow backend (50ms)
                       ▼
                    balance Rs.1,000,000 → store in cache → return

  guest.withdraw(...) → invoke(method=withdraw)
    │ role != TELLER
    ▼ throw SecurityException  (real service never called)

  Spring AOP analogy:
    bean call → Spring-generated proxy → advice (@Transactional) → real method
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Proxy Pattern & Types ═══

  ┌─ Proxy Types ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Virtual    : lazy-create expensive object on first use         │
  │ Protection : access control before delegating (role check)     │
  │ Caching    : return cached result on repeat calls              │
  │ Remote     : stand-in for object in another JVM/host (RMI/RPC) │
  │ Dynamic/JDK: Proxy.newProxyInstance + InvocationHandler        │
  │ (CGLIB)    : subclass proxy when no interface (not final)      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>>        │◀───────│ RealAccountService        │ (real subject)
  │ AccountService       │ impl    │ + getBalance / withdraw   │
  │ + getBalance(id)     │        └───────────────────────────┘
  │ + withdraw(id,amt)   │◀───────┐
  └──────────────────────┘ impl    │
                                   │ (generated at runtime)
                          ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                          │ $Proxy → InvocationHandler     │
                          │ CachingSecurityHandler         │
                          │ - target: AccountService ◇     │
                          │ - role: String                 │
                          │ - cache: Map                   │
                          │ + invoke(proxy, method, args)  │
                          └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. proxy.getBalance("SAV2001")
  2.   invoke(getBalance) → cache miss → method.invoke(real)
  3.   store + return 1,000,000
  4. proxy.getBalance("SAV2001") → cache HIT → return (no backend)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Proxy pattern provides a stand-in for another object to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real object, so clients cannot tell they are talking to a surrogate, but the proxy can add behaviour before or after delegating to the real object. There are several standard types. A virtual proxy lazily creates an expensive object only when first needed. A protection proxy enforces access control before delegating. A caching proxy returns cached results on repeat calls. A remote proxy represents an object in another process or machine and hides the networking, as Java RMI stubs do. And a smart proxy adds things like logging or lock management around access.

In Java, proxies come in two forms. A static proxy is a class you write by hand. A dynamic proxy is generated at runtime — the JDK dynamic proxy uses Proxy.newProxyInstance with an InvocationHandler, routing every method call through an invoke method where you add behaviour and then delegate. The key limitation is that JDK dynamic proxies need the target to implement an interface, because the generated proxy implements interfaces; when there is no interface, Spring falls back to CGLIB, which generates a subclass, so it cannot proxy final classes or methods.

This is exactly how Spring AOP works, which is the part I emphasise. When I annotate a method with @Transactional, @Cacheable, or @Async, Spring does not change my class. At startup it wraps my bean in a proxy — a JDK dynamic proxy if the bean implements an interface, otherwise a CGLIB subclass proxy. When another bean calls my method, it really calls the proxy, which runs the advice around my method, so for @Transactional it opens a transaction, commits on success, and rolls back on an exception, then delegates to my real method. My business code stays clean and the cross-cutting concern is added by the proxy.

In my banking project I used this idea directly by wrapping the account service in a dynamic proxy that added a short-lived balance cache and a role-based access check, so repeated balance lookups were served from cache and only a teller could withdraw, all without editing the real service. The one trap I always warn about is self-invocation: if a bean calls another of its own methods with plain this, the call does not go through the proxy, so a @Transactional or @Cacheable annotation on that inner method silently does nothing. I fix that by calling the annotated method from a different bean, injecting the bean into itself, or using AopContext.currentProxy — and knowing this explains a whole class of confusing Spring bugs.

answers.question: What is the difference between the Facade pattern (new simple interface over complex subsystems) and the Adapter pattern (make one incompatible interface match another)?
answers.shortTitle: Facade pattern vs Adapter pattern — a simple interface over a subsystem vs making incompatible interfaces match

s1_definition.profdef: The Facade pattern provides a single, simplified interface over a complex subsystem of many classes, hiding their interactions so clients deal with one easy entry point. The Adapter pattern converts the interface of an existing class into another interface that a client expects, so two otherwise incompatible types can work together. The core difference is intent: Facade simplifies and unifies a complex set of collaborating classes you own, while Adapter translates one specific existing interface into a different one the client requires, usually to integrate code you cannot change.
s1_definition.analogy: A facade is like the single relationship manager at National Bank of India who handles Rajesh's whole request. Behind her are many departments — accounts, loans, cards, compliance — but Rajesh only talks to her, and she coordinates all of them. She gives him one simple door into a complicated building. An adapter is different: imagine Rajesh brings a foreign credit-score report in a format the bank's loan software cannot read. The bank uses a small translator that converts that foreign report into the exact format the loan software expects. The adapter does not simplify a whole building; it makes one specific incompatible thing fit a specific socket.
s1_definition.oneliner: Facade gives one simple front door to a complex subsystem; Adapter translates one incompatible interface into the one the client expects.

sections.s2_technical:
The **Facade** pattern is about simplification and decoupling. You have a subsystem of many classes that must be used together in a particular sequence, with tricky interdependencies. A facade is a single class that exposes a small number of high-level methods and, inside, orchestrates all the subsystem classes in the right order. The client talks only to the facade, so it is shielded from the subsystem's complexity and from changes inside it. For example, opening an account really involves a KYC service, an account repository, a card issuer, and a notification service, each with several steps. A facade `AccountOpeningFacade.openAccount(request)` runs all of them in order and returns one result, so controllers call one method instead of coordinating four services. Importantly, a facade does not hide the subsystem — advanced clients can still use the subsystem classes directly if they need to; the facade just offers the easy common path. The intent is to reduce coupling and complexity for the common case.

The **Adapter** pattern is about compatibility. You have an existing class, often third-party or legacy, whose interface does not match what your client code expects. An adapter sits between them and translates calls from the expected interface into calls the existing class understands. There are two flavours. An **object adapter** holds a reference to the adaptee and delegates to it — this is the common, composition-based form. A **class adapter** uses multiple inheritance of interfaces to adapt, which in Java means implementing the target interface while extending the adaptee, and is less flexible. For example, your loan system expects a `CreditScoreProvider` interface with `int getScore(String pan)`, but a vendor library exposes `CibilApi.fetch(request)` returning a different object. A `CibilAdapter implements CreditScoreProvider` wraps the vendor API, translating `getScore` into the vendor's call and converting the result. The client sees only the `CreditScoreProvider` interface and never knows about the vendor's shape.

Now the differences, stated clearly. **Intent** is the biggest one: Facade simplifies a complex subsystem into an easier interface, while Adapter makes an existing interface compatible with a different required one. **Number of objects**: a facade typically fronts many subsystem classes, whereas an adapter usually wraps a single adaptee to match a single target interface. **Interface design**: with a facade you design a brand-new convenient interface of your choosing, driven by what makes the client's life easy; with an adapter the target interface already exists and is fixed, and you must conform the adaptee to it. **When you reach for them**: you add a facade when a subsystem is getting painful to use and you want one clean entry point, often during design of your own code; you add an adapter when you must integrate something whose interface you cannot or do not want to change, often a library or legacy system. **Change over time**: a facade is proactive simplification you plan, while an adapter is often reactive glue to bridge a mismatch you discovered.

A senior nuance is that both are structural patterns and both wrap other objects, which is why juniors confuse them. The way I keep them straight is to ask: am I simplifying many things into one easy interface (Facade), or am I converting one thing into a different expected interface (Adapter)? Real Java examples help: `java.util.Arrays.asList` adapts an array to the `List` interface (Adapter), and the SLF4J bindings adapt one logging API to another (Adapter), while a service class that wraps several repositories and clients to offer one business operation is effectively a Facade. They can even coexist — a facade might internally use adapters to talk to incompatible subsystem pieces.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, opening an account requires calling a KYC checker, saving the account, issuing a card, and sending a welcome notification, each a separate class with its own steps and ordering rules. Controllers that wanted to open an account had to know and coordinate all four, which was error-prone and duplicated across the codebase. This is the problem Facade solves — we create one `AccountOpeningFacade` with a single `openAccount` method that orchestrates the four services, so callers use one simple method.

Problem 2 — The loan part of the same flow needs a credit score, and the bank uses a third-party CIBIL library whose method signature and return type do not match our internal `CreditScoreProvider` interface. We cannot change the vendor library. This is the problem Adapter solves — we write a `CibilAdapter` that implements our `CreditScoreProvider` and translates to the vendor's API, so our code depends only on our own interface.

In the mini-project we will build both patterns side by side so the contrast is obvious. We will create the four subsystem services and an `AccountOpeningFacade` that coordinates them. We will also create the vendor-style `CibilLegacyApi` with a mismatched interface and a `CibilAdapter` that makes it fit our `CreditScoreProvider`. The `main` will open an account for Rajesh through the facade, and inside that flow the facade will obtain a credit score through the adapter, showing how a facade can even use an adapter internally.

The code contains: four subsystem services; an `AccountOpeningFacade`; a `CreditScoreProvider` interface; a mismatched `CibilLegacyApi`; a `CibilAdapter`; and a `main` that runs the full flow.

Input data: an account-opening request for Rajesh, account SAV2001, PAN ABCDE1234F.

Step 1: We create the adapter first, wrapping the vendor `CibilLegacyApi` inside a `CibilAdapter` that implements our `CreditScoreProvider` interface. Our code will only ever see the clean `getScore` method, not the vendor's `fetch`.

Step 2: We create the `AccountOpeningFacade`, passing in the four subsystem services and the credit provider. The facade is the single simple front door over all of them.

Step 3: A caller invokes `facade.openAccount` — one method call. Inside, the facade first asks the KYC service to verify the PAN, which succeeds.

Step 4: The facade calls `credit.getScore(pan)`. This goes through the adapter, which builds a vendor request, calls the vendor's `fetch`, receives the vendor's response with a letter rating and a numeric band, and translates it into the plain integer our code expects. The facade logs the score. This shows a facade using an adapter internally.

Step 5: The facade then creates the account, issues a card, and sends a welcome message, in the correct order. The caller did none of this coordination — the facade hid it all behind one method. The two patterns played distinct roles: the facade simplified the whole flow, and the adapter made one incompatible dependency fit.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Facade pattern and the Adapter pattern are both structural patterns that wrap other objects, which is why they are easily confused, but their intent is completely different. A facade provides a single simplified interface over a complex subsystem of many classes, hiding their interactions so the client deals with one easy entry point. An adapter converts the interface of an existing class into a different interface that the client expects, so two otherwise incompatible types can work together.

The cleanest way I distinguish them is by asking one question: am I simplifying many collaborating classes into one convenient interface, or am I translating one specific thing into a different expected interface? If it is simplification over a subsystem, it is a facade. If it is translation to achieve compatibility, it is an adapter. There are also practical differences. A facade usually fronts many subsystem classes and lets me design a brand-new convenient interface of my choosing, while an adapter typically wraps a single adaptee and must conform to a target interface that already exists and is fixed. I reach for a facade proactively when a subsystem is painful to use, and I reach for an adapter reactively when I must integrate a library or legacy system whose interface I cannot change.

In my banking project the account-opening flow used both. Opening an account required a KYC check, saving the account, issuing a card, and sending a welcome message, each a separate service with ordering rules. I created an AccountOpeningFacade with a single openAccount method that orchestrated all four, so controllers called one method instead of coordinating four services. That is a facade simplifying a subsystem.

Inside that same flow I needed a credit score from a third-party CIBIL library whose method name and return type did not match our internal CreditScoreProvider interface, and I could not change the vendor library. So I wrote a CibilAdapter that implemented our interface and, inside, translated our getScore call into the vendor's fetch call and converted the vendor's response into the plain integer our code expected. That is an adapter achieving compatibility. The nice detail is that the facade used the adapter internally, which shows the patterns are complementary — the facade simplified the whole flow while the adapter bridged one incompatible dependency. A couple of standard Java examples I cite are Arrays.asList adapting an array to the List interface and SLF4J bindings adapting one logging API to another, both adapters, while any service class that wraps several repositories and clients to expose one business operation is effectively a facade.

answers.question: How do you approach a low-level design question (e.g. design a Parking Lot, Car Rental, or Elevator system) — identify actors, extract core entities (the nouns), assign single responsibilities, define relationships and interfaces, and apply patterns only where they solve a real problem?
answers.shortTitle: How to approach a low-level design question (identify actors, extract entities, assign responsibilities, apply patterns)

s1_definition.profdef: A low-level design question asks you to produce the class-level design of a bounded system — the entities, their fields and methods, the relationships between them, the interfaces, and the key patterns. A disciplined approach is to clarify requirements and constraints, identify the actors who interact with the system, extract the core entities by finding the important nouns, assign each entity a single clear responsibility, define relationships and interfaces between them, and apply design patterns only where they solve a genuine problem rather than for show. The goal is a cohesive, extensible object model, not a premature framework.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India asks you to design a safe-deposit-locker system. You do not start coding. First you ask who uses it — customers like Rajesh, bank staff, an auditor — these are the actors. Then you list the important things involved — Locker, Vault, Customer, Booking, Payment — these are the nouns, your entities. Then you give each thing one clear job — the Locker knows its size and status, the Vault manages lockers, the Booking links a customer to a locker for a period. Then you decide how they connect — a Vault has many Lockers, a Booking references one Locker and one Customer. Only then, if a real need appears, you reach for a pattern — for example a Strategy for different pricing tiers. You design the model before you write a line of logic.
s1_definition.oneliner: Clarify requirements, find the actors, extract the noun entities, give each one responsibility, define relationships and interfaces, and add patterns only where they earn their place.

**Professional definition:** A low-level design question asks you to produce the class-level design of a bounded system — the entities, their fields and methods, the relationships between them, the interfaces, and the key patterns. A disciplined approach is to clarify requirements and constraints, identify the actors who interact with the system, extract the core entities by finding the important nouns, assign each entity a single clear responsibility, define relationships and interfaces between them, and apply design patterns only where they solve a genuine problem rather than for show. The goal is a cohesive, extensible object model, not a premature framework.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India asks you to design a safe-deposit-locker system. You do not start coding. First you ask who uses it — customers like Rajesh, bank staff, an auditor — these are the actors. Then you list the important things involved — Locker, Vault, Customer, Booking, Payment — these are the nouns, your entities. Then you give each thing one clear job — the Locker knows its size and status, the Vault manages lockers, the Booking links a customer to a locker for a period. Then you decide how they connect — a Vault has many Lockers, a Booking references one Locker and one Customer. Only then, if a real need appears, you reach for a pattern — for example a Strategy for different pricing tiers. You design the model before you write a line of logic.

**One line to remember:** Clarify requirements, find the actors, extract the noun entities, give each one responsibility, define relationships and interfaces, and add patterns only where they earn their place.

sections.s2_technical:
The first step is to **clarify requirements and scope**. Interviewers deliberately leave LLD questions vague to see whether you ask. You pin down the functional requirements (what the system must do), the constraints (sizes, limits, concurrency), and explicitly what is out of scope. For a parking lot you would ask: how many levels, what vehicle types, is payment included, is it single-threaded or concurrent. Writing down scope prevents you from designing the wrong thing.

Second, **identify the actors**. Actors are the people or external systems that interact with the system. For a parking lot they are the driver, the admin, and perhaps a payment gateway. Actors reveal the entry points and the operations the system must expose, which later become your public methods.

Third, **extract the core entities by finding the nouns**. Read the requirements and underline the important nouns: ParkingLot, Level, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, Payment. These become your classes. This noun-extraction technique is a reliable way to discover the domain model. You then add the key attributes (fields) for each — a ParkingSpot has a spot number, a size, and an occupied flag.

Fourth, **assign single responsibilities**. Each class should do one job, following the Single Responsibility Principle. The ParkingSpot tracks its own state, the Level manages its spots, the ParkingLot coordinates levels and issues tickets, and a separate PaymentProcessor handles money. Resist the temptation to create a God class that does everything; split responsibilities so each class has one clear reason to change.

Fifth, **define relationships and interfaces**. Decide how entities relate — a ParkingLot has many Levels (composition, they die together), a Level has many ParkingSpots, a Ticket references one Vehicle and one Spot. Choose the right relationship: composition for owns-and-dies-together, aggregation for has-but-independent, inheritance only for genuine is-a relationships, and composition over inheritance when in doubt. Introduce interfaces where you expect variation, such as a `PricingStrategy` or a `Vehicle` abstraction with Car, Bike, and Truck subtypes. Add multiplicities — one lot to many levels, one ticket to one spot.

Sixth, **apply patterns only where they solve a real problem**. This is the maturity signal interviewers look for. Use a Strategy for pricing that genuinely varies, a Factory if object creation is complex and centralised, a State pattern or guarded enum for an entity with a real lifecycle, an Observer if several things must react to an event. But do not force patterns. Adding a pattern that solves no real problem is over-engineering and a red flag. The right answer is often the simplest cohesive model, with a pattern introduced precisely where variation or complexity justifies it.

A few senior nuances. Keep orchestration logic thin and let entities own their own state transitions — the ParkingSpot should decide how it becomes occupied, not have the lot reach in and flip a flag. Think about concurrency if the problem implies it: assigning a spot in a busy lot needs synchronisation or atomic operations so two cars do not get the same spot. Make the model extensible for the inevitable follow-up "how would you add electric-vehicle charging spots?" — a good model answers that by adding a subtype or a new strategy, not by rewriting existing classes, which is the Open/Closed Principle. And always sanity-check the design by tracing a concrete scenario end to end, which exposes missing methods or awkward relationships before the interviewer finds them.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a safe-deposit-locker management system for its branch. Staff kept a messy spreadsheet, so lockers were double-booked and nobody knew which were free. We need a clean object model that tracks lockers of different sizes, assigns a free locker of the requested size to a customer, and prices the booking. This is a classic low-level design task, and we will apply the exact method: clarify scope, find actors, extract nouns, assign responsibilities, define relationships, and add a pattern only where pricing genuinely varies.

Problem 2 — Pricing differs by locker size (small, medium, large) and the bank will add more tiers later. Hard-coding a pricing if-else would violate Open/Closed. This is the one place a Strategy pattern genuinely earns its keep, so we introduce a `PricingStrategy`. Everywhere else we keep the model simple and avoid forcing patterns.

In the mini-project we will model the locker system. Entities (the nouns): `Locker`, `LockerVault`, `Customer`, `Booking`, and a `PricingStrategy` interface with per-size implementations. Responsibilities: the `Locker` owns its size and occupied state and its own assign/release transitions; the `LockerVault` manages the collection and finds a free locker; the `Booking` links a customer to a locker and holds the price. The `main` will book a medium locker for Rajesh and a large one for Priya, show pricing via the strategy, and show that no free locker of a size leads to a clean failure.

The code contains: the entities with single responsibilities, the pricing strategy, and a demo that traces a booking end to end.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a vault with three lockers (small, medium, large), and booking requests from Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: We clarified scope (single branch, three sizes, assign-one-free-locker, price by size) and identified actors (customers and, implicitly, staff). From the nouns we created the entities: Locker, Customer, Booking, LockerVault, and a PricingStrategy. Each has one responsibility.

Step 2: The vault is populated with three lockers. The vault owns the lockers (composition) and knows how to find a free one, while each locker owns its own occupied state.

Step 3: Rajesh requests a MEDIUM locker. The vault scans its lockers, finds L2 free and medium, calls `l.assign()` so the locker flips its own state to occupied, asks the pricing strategy for the medium price of three thousand, and returns a Booking linking Rajesh, L2, and the price.

Step 4: Priya requests a LARGE locker. The vault finds L3 free and large, assigns it, prices it at five thousand, and returns the booking.

Step 5: Priya then requests another MEDIUM locker, but L2 is already occupied and there is no other medium. The vault finds none free of that size and returns null, which the caller handles as a clean "no locker available" rather than a crash. Tracing this scenario end to end confirms the model has the right methods and relationships, and it makes the Open/Closed extension obvious: adding an EXTRA_LARGE size is a new pricing case and new lockers, not a rewrite.

```
2026-10-26 10:45:00 [INFO] === Book lockers (LLD model traced end to end) ===

2026-10-26 10:45:00 [INFO] Booked L3 for Priya @ Rs.5000
2026-10-26 10:45:00 [INFO] === No free MEDIUM left -> clean failure ===
2026-10-26 10:45:00 [WARNING] No free MEDIUM locker available
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I get a low-level design question like design a parking lot, a car rental, or a locker system, I follow a disciplined sequence rather than jumping into code. First I clarify requirements and scope, because these questions are deliberately vague and the interviewer wants to see me ask about vehicle types, sizes, limits, whether payment is included, and whether it is concurrent. Writing down scope stops me designing the wrong thing.

Then I identify the actors — the people or systems that interact with it, like the driver, the admin, and a payment gateway — because actors reveal the operations the system must expose. Next I extract the core entities by underlining the important nouns in the requirements, so ParkingLot, Level, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, and Payment become my classes, and I give each its key fields. After that I assign each class a single responsibility, resisting the God class — the spot tracks its own state, the level manages its spots, the lot coordinates and issues tickets, and a separate processor handles money.

Then I define relationships and interfaces: composition for owns-and-dies-together like a lot and its levels, aggregation for has-but-independent, inheritance only for a true is-a, and I favour composition over inheritance. I introduce interfaces where I genuinely expect variation, such as a pricing strategy or a vehicle abstraction. Only after the model is solid do I apply design patterns, and crucially only where they solve a real problem — a Strategy for pricing that truly varies, a Factory if creation is complex, a guarded enum or State for a real lifecycle. Forcing patterns that solve nothing is over-engineering and a red flag.

In my banking project I used exactly this method to design the safe-deposit-locker system. The nouns gave me Locker, LockerVault, Customer, and Booking, I let each locker own its own occupied state while the vault handled assignment, and I introduced a PricingStrategy only because pricing genuinely varied by size, keeping everything else simple. I always finish by tracing a concrete scenario end to end to expose missing methods, I think about concurrency where the problem implies it so two requests cannot grab the same resource, and I make sure the model answers the inevitable follow-up how would you extend this by adding a new subtype or strategy rather than rewriting existing classes, which is the Open/Closed Principle in action.

answers.question: In LLD, how do you model state and behavior cleanly (enums + guarded state transitions vs the full State pattern), when do you use inheritance vs composition for type variants (e.g. vehicle types), and why keep orchestration in a thin service while entities own their own state transitions?
answers.shortTitle: Modeling state and behavior cleanly — guarded enum transitions vs the State pattern, inheritance vs composition, and thin services

s1_definition.profdef: Clean state-and-behaviour modelling means an entity's lifecycle is represented explicitly and only legal transitions are allowed. For simple lifecycles you use an enum of states plus guarded transition logic that rejects illegal moves; for complex lifecycles where each state has substantial, differing behaviour you use the full State pattern, giving each state its own class. For type variants you prefer composition over inheritance unless there is a genuine is-a relationship with shared behaviour. And you keep orchestration logic in a thin service layer while entities own their own state transitions, so business rules live close to the data they govern.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a loan at National Bank of India. A loan moves through stages: applied, under review, approved, disbursed, closed — or rejected. You want to make sure nobody can jump from applied straight to disbursed without approval. If the stages are simple, you just keep a status label and a small rule that says which moves are allowed — that is the guarded enum approach. If each stage had rich, very different behaviour, you would give each stage its own expert desk that knows exactly what to do — that is the State pattern. For the kinds of loan (home, car, personal), you ask whether they are genuinely different species sharing a core (inheritance) or just the same loan with different settings (composition). And the loan itself should know how to move from approved to disbursed; the manager (service) just says "disburse it," keeping the manager thin.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a guarded enum for simple lifecycles and the State pattern for rich ones, prefer composition over inheritance for variants, and let entities own their transitions while the service stays thin.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with **enums plus guarded transitions** for simple state. You model the states as an enum, for example `enum LoanStatus { APPLIED, UNDER_REVIEW, APPROVED, DISBURSED, CLOSED, REJECTED }`. The entity holds its current status and exposes transition methods that check whether the move is legal before changing. For example `void approve() { if (status != UNDER_REVIEW) throw new IllegalStateException("can only approve a loan under review"); status = APPROVED; }`. The guard is the key — it prevents illegal transitions like approving a closed loan. You can centralise the legal moves in a small map of allowed transitions if there are many. This approach is simple, readable, and perfect when the behaviour attached to each state is small; the difference between states is mostly which transitions are allowed, not big chunks of distinct logic.

Move to the **full State pattern** when each state carries substantial and genuinely different behaviour. In the State pattern you define a state interface with the operations, and each concrete state is its own class implementing those operations differently, plus deciding the next state. The context object delegates to its current state object. You reach for this when a long if-else or switch on the status keeps appearing in many methods, when each state's behaviour is complex, or when adding a new state should be adding a class rather than editing switches everywhere. The trade-off is more classes and indirection, so you do not use it for a trivial three-state lifecycle where a guarded enum is clearer. The rule of thumb: guarded enum for simple state-machines where behaviour per state is thin; State pattern when per-state behaviour is rich and varied.

For **type variants, prefer composition over inheritance**, and use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship with meaningful shared behaviour. Take vehicle types or loan types. Inheritance is tempting — `HomeLoan extends Loan`, `CarLoan extends Loan`. It is appropriate only if the subtypes are genuinely specialised kinds that share real behaviour and honour the Liskov Substitution Principle, meaning a subtype works anywhere the parent is expected without breaking the contract. But inheritance is rigid: it is single-inheritance in Java, it tightly couples subclass to superclass internals, and it handles combinations poorly. If the variation is really about differing data or pluggable behaviour — interest rules, tenure limits, eligibility — composition is better: the loan holds a `LoanType` value or a `InterestStrategy` object rather than being a subclass. Composition lets you mix and change behaviour at runtime and avoids a brittle hierarchy. The guideline most engineers follow is favour composition over inheritance, and reserve inheritance for stable, genuine is-a hierarchies.

Finally, **thin service and entities own their transitions**. A common anti-pattern is the anaemic domain model, where entities are just bags of getters and setters and all the logic lives in a fat service that reaches in and mutates fields directly, for example `loan.setStatus(APPROVED)`. This scatters business rules away from the data and lets any caller set an illegal status. The cleaner design puts the transition logic inside the entity — `loan.approve()` enforces its own guard — so the rules live with the data and cannot be bypassed. The service then stays thin: it coordinates the use case (load the loan, call `loan.approve()`, save it, publish an event) but does not contain the state rules themselves. This keeps the domain model rich and the service focused on orchestration, which is easier to test and far harder to misuse. In a banking system this matters enormously because an illegal state transition on a loan or an account can mean real financial error.

A senior nuance: entities owning transitions pairs naturally with persistence — you load the entity, invoke a behaviour, and save it, and the entity guarantees it is never in an illegal state. And when the lifecycle genuinely grows complex, you can refactor the guarded-enum entity into a State pattern without changing the service, because the service only calls high-level methods like `approve()` regardless of how the state is implemented underneath.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes loans with a clear lifecycle: applied, under review, approved, disbursed, closed, or rejected. In the old code, a fat `LoanService` set the status directly with setters, so a bug once disbursed a loan that had never been approved, causing a real financial incident. We need the loan to own its transitions and reject illegal moves, with the service kept thin. Because the per-state behaviour here is simple — mostly about which transitions are legal — a guarded enum is the right tool, not the heavier State pattern.

Problem 2 — The bank offers home, car, and personal loans that differ mainly in interest rate and maximum tenure, not in fundamentally different behaviour. Modelling these as a deep subclass hierarchy would be brittle, so we use composition: the loan holds a loan-type configuration rather than being a subclass. This demonstrates choosing composition over inheritance for variants.

In the mini-project we will model a `Loan` entity that owns its status and exposes guarded transition methods (`startReview`, `approve`, `disburse`, `reject`) that throw on illegal moves. We will use a `LoanType` composed value for rate and tenure rather than subclasses. A thin `LoanService` will orchestrate a use case — submit, review, approve, disburse — calling the entity's methods, never setting status directly. We will run a valid lifecycle for Rajesh and then attempt an illegal jump (disburse before approve) to show the guard rejecting it.

The code contains: a `LoanStatus` enum; a composed `LoanType`; a `Loan` entity owning guarded transitions; a thin `LoanService`; and a demo of a valid flow plus a blocked illegal transition.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's home loan of thirty lakh going through a valid lifecycle, and Priya's car loan where we try an illegal jump.

Step 1: The service submits Rajesh's loan. A `Loan` entity is created with a composed `LoanType` for home (rate and tenure), and its status starts at APPLIED. The variant data lives inside the loan as a value, not as a subclass, which is composition over inheritance.

Step 2: The service calls `review`, which simply calls `loan.startReview()`. Inside the entity, the guard checks the status is APPLIED, then moves it to UNDER_REVIEW. The rule lives in the entity, not the service.

Step 3: The service calls `approve`. The entity's guard checks the status is UNDER_REVIEW, then moves to APPROVED, logging the loan type and rate from the composed value.

Step 4: The service calls `disburse`. The entity checks the status is APPROVED and moves to DISBURSED. The whole legal path worked, and at no point did the service set a status directly.

Step 5: For Priya's car loan, still APPLIED, the service calls `disburse`. The entity's guard sees the status is APPLIED, not APPROVED, and throws an `IllegalStateException`. The illegal jump that once caused a real incident is now impossible, because the entity owns and enforces its transitions while the service stays thin.

```
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [INFO] LN-1 -> UNDER_REVIEW
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [INFO] LN-1 -> APPROVED (HOME @ 0.085)
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [INFO] LN-1 -> DISBURSED Rs.3000000
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [INFO] === Illegal transition is rejected by the entity ===
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [INFO] Submitted LN-2 for CUR3001 Rs.800000
2026-10-26 10:50:00 [WARNING] Blocked illegal transition: cannot disburse from APPLIED (must be APPROVED)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
For modelling state and behaviour cleanly in a low-level design, my first decision is how rich the lifecycle is. If the states are simple and the difference between them is mostly about which transitions are legal, I use an enum of states plus guarded transition methods on the entity. Each transition method checks the current state and throws if the move is illegal, so something like approving a loan is only allowed from the under-review state. If instead each state carries substantial, genuinely different behaviour, and I keep seeing big switch statements on the status across many methods, I upgrade to the full State pattern, giving each state its own class that implements the operations and decides the next state. The trade-off is that the State pattern adds classes and indirection, so I do not use it for a trivial three-state lifecycle where a guarded enum is clearer.

For type variants like vehicle types or loan types, I prefer composition over inheritance. Inheritance is only appropriate for a genuine is-a relationship with meaningful shared behaviour that honours Liskov substitution. If the variation is really about differing data or pluggable behaviour — interest rates, tenure limits, eligibility rules — I model it as composition, so the loan holds a loan-type value or a strategy object rather than being a subclass. Composition avoids a brittle single-inheritance hierarchy, handles combinations better, and lets me change behaviour at runtime.

The third principle I always apply is keeping the service thin while the entity owns its transitions. The anti-pattern is an anaemic domain model where entities are just getters and setters and a fat service sets the status directly, which scatters business rules and lets callers create illegal states. Instead I put the transition logic inside the entity, so calling approve enforces its own guard and the status can never be bypassed. The service then only orchestrates the use case — load the entity, call the behaviour, save it, publish an event — which is easier to test and much harder to misuse.

In my banking project this mattered directly. A fat loan service once set a status with a setter and disbursed a loan that had never been approved, causing a real financial incident. I refactored so the loan entity owned guarded transitions and rejected illegal moves, used a composed loan-type value instead of a subclass hierarchy, and kept the service thin. The illegal jump became impossible. And because the service only calls high-level methods like approve, I could later refactor the internal state implementation from a guarded enum to a State pattern without touching the service at all, which is exactly the flexibility good modelling gives you.
